bridge_paragraph: SugarCRM uses a PHP-based module architecture with Accounts, Contacts, Leads, Opportunities, and custom modules stored in a MySQL/MariaDB database, while Salesforce uses a cloud-native object model with stricter typing, validation rules, and the AppExchange ecosystem. Mine translates Sugar's open-source CRM data to Salesforce's enterprise platform automatically.
overview_paragraphs: SugarCRM to Salesforce is a legacy CRM upgrade migration. Companies move from SugarCRM (including SugarCRM Enterprise, Sugar Sell, and older Community Edition deployments) to Salesforce for the ecosystem, AppExchange marketplace, Einstein AI, and the breadth of Salesforce's platform. This migration is common when companies outgrow Sugar's capabilities, when self-hosted Sugar instances become maintenance burdens, or when companies want cloud-native CRM without managing infrastructure.

The migration maps Sugar's module-based architecture to Salesforce's object model. The core concepts are similar — both have Leads, Contacts, Accounts, and Opportunities — but field types, relationship patterns, and customization mechanisms differ. Sugar's Studio customizations (custom fields, layouts, relationships) must be translated to Salesforce's custom fields, page layouts, and Lightning components. Sugar's workflow rules become Salesforce Flows.
Companies typically use Salesforce Data Loader with CSV exports from Sugar's database. The custom module mapping and workflow translation require manual analysis.

challenges.title: Sugar custom modules to Salesforce custom objects
challenges.description: SugarCRM's Module Builder creates custom modules with fields, relationships, and layouts. These map to Salesforce custom objects but with different relationship patterns — Sugar's flex-relate fields, one-to-many, and many-to-many relationships need Salesforce lookup, master-detail, or junction object equivalents.

challenges.title: Workflow to Salesforce Flow translation

challenges.title: Self-hosted data extraction

how_mine_helps: Mine profiles Sugar's database schema (including custom module tables and relationship join tables) and generates Salesforce object mappings with field-level type translation.

Sugar's flex-relate fields and many-to-many relationships (stored in *_cstm and relationship tables) are translated to Salesforce lookups, master-detail, or junction objects.
Mine catalogs all Sugar workflow and process definitions, documenting field references and trigger conditions for Salesforce Flow rebuilding.

overview_paragraphs: Legacy HR database to Workday migrations happen when companies replace homegrown or obsolete HRIS systems. The source might be a custom SQL database built 15 years ago, an Access-based employee tracking system, a FileMaker payroll application, or a collection of spreadsheets that function as HR records. Companies make this move when the legacy system's developer leaves, when compliance requirements exceed the system's capabilities, or when the company reaches a size where a proper HCM platform is necessary.

Every legacy HR migration is unique because there's no standard schema. Employee data may be spread across multiple tables with no obvious join path. Job history might be a single 'current job' field with no historical tracking. Pay data might mix salary, hourly, and contractor records in one table. Benefits enrollment might be tracked in spreadsheets entirely outside the database. Mine's value is in the discovery phase — understanding what's in the database before you can map it.
Companies typically hire an HR consultant and a database developer to reverse-engineer the schema. This manual approach takes 4–8 months for HR databases with 20–100 tables.
